quantities.label: A corridor, not a hill

quantity.scope: Communes in the Saint-Joseph geographic area recorded by the specification

quantities.statement: The geographic area covers 26 communes — 23 in the Ardèche and three in the Loire — strung over roughly sixty kilometres of right bank. One appellation name therefore covers a long sequence of different slopes rather than a single côte.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Saint-Joseph was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 15 June 1956, the last of the eight crus to be created; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: Two colours, three grapes
sections.statement: Saint-Joseph may be red or white. For reds the specification requires Syrah to be at least 90% of the holding's encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne permitted only as accessory varieties in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 10% of the vines, and wines made from both colours must be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés". Whites come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: An outline that moved twice
sections.statement: The specification records Saint-Joseph beginning in 1956 on six communes around Tournon, expanding in 1969 by twenty further communes reaching north to the Condrieu area, and then being significantly narrowed by parcel revisions approved on 9–10 February 1994 and 20 June 2018, which cut the delimited parcel area from about 6,800 to about 3,400 hectares. Today's outline is a made thing, not a timeless one.

quantity.scope: Jurançon geographic production area described by INAO

quantities.statement: INAO describes the Jurançon production area across 25 communes between Pau and the Pyrenees.

quantities.label: Member vineyards

quantity.scope: Vignerons du Jurançon association member vineyards; not total AOP vineyard area

quantities.statement: The Vignerons du Jurançon association reports 620 hectares of member vineyards; this is not represented as the total AOP vineyard area.

sections.statement: Béarn is the historical and cultural foothill world around Pau; CARTA keeps it distinct from Béarn AOP and uses Jurançon as the clearest mapped route into its white-wine culture.

sections.label: Why this world matters
sections.statement: The Béarn–Jurançon world makes the relationship between mountain foothills, long autumn ripening, local Manseng grapes and both dry and sweet white wine unusually legible.

sections.label: Jurançon landscape
sections.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

sections.label: Dry + sweet
sections.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

sections.label: Three legal paths
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

sections.label: Principal + accessory grapes
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

sections.label: Harvest changes the path
sections.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

sections.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
sections.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.statement: Burgundy is a long, fragmented wine region whose identity is read through nested origin: regional appellations, village wines, Premier Cru sites and Grand Cru appellations.

sections.label: Why Burgundy matters

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Condrieu was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 27 April 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: Condrieu is a still white wine and its specification states plainly that "les vins sont issus du cépage viognier B" — Viognier and nothing else.

sections.label: Sweetness is a range
sections.statement: The specification's own account describes a wine that was doux in the mid-nineteenth century and is in most cases sec, sometimes demi-sec, in its modern form, with confidential quantities of moelleux or doux made from overripe grapes when conditions allow. "Dry white Viognier" is therefore the usual case, not the legal definition.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area runs across seven communes and three departments: Condrieu in the Rhône; Chavanay, Malleval, Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf and Vérin in the Loire; and Limony in the Ardèche. INAO gives the vineyard as roughly 100 hectares of terraced right-bank hillside.

sections.label: Near-disappearance and recovery
sections.statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Cornas was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 5 August 1938; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

sections.label: The amphitheatre
sections.statement: The specification describes most of the vineyard as sitting on soils weathered from primary eruptive rock of the granite family — the porphyritic granites of Tournon — in an amphitheatre open to the south and sheltered from the north by the Arlettes massif, terraced behind stone walls.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Crozes-Hermitage was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 4 March 1937; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 10 December 2024.

sections.label: Two colours, three grapes
sections.statement: Crozes-Hermitage may be red or white. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne admitted as accessory varieties in mixed plantings up to 15% of the vines; whites are Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area covers eleven Drôme communes on the left bank facing Tournon — Beaumont-Monteux, Chanos-Curson, Crozes-Hermitage, Erôme, Gervans, Larnage, Pont-de-l'Isère, La Roche-de-Glun, Serves-sur-Rhône, Tain-l'Hermitage and part of Mercurol-Veaunes. It is the largest of the eight crus and the least uniform.

sections.label: Two different grounds
sections.statement: The specification splits the appellation in two. In the north the Rhône has cut down to the granite de Tournon between Crozes-Hermitage and Serves-sur-Rhône, and sandy clays and granitic arenas are held on the slopes by dry-stone terraces. In the south and east lie Quaternary terraces of alpine gravels, with loess locally at the Gervans quartier of Les Blancs and distinctive kaolin sands at Larnage.

sections.label: One commune becomes eleven
sections.statement: The 1937 decree limited the area to part of the single commune of Crozes-Hermitage; postwar prosperity and vineyard expansion took it to eleven communes by 1952. A later reselection of the parcels from which grapes may come cut the production potential from 4,800 to 3,200 hectares.

sections.label: Where geology and law disagree
sections.statement: The Crozes-Hermitage specification identifies its northern granite as the same formation that appears across the Rhône around Tournon, in Saint-Joseph. Geology crosses the river and the appellation boundary; the law does not.

sections.statement: Jura is a compact eastern French wine region whose six wine AOPs form three overlapping families: geographic still-wine origins, traditional-method Crémant du Jura, and fortified Macvin du Jura.

sections.label: Why Jura matters
sections.statement: Jura makes legal hierarchy, grape identity and winemaking method unusually easy to compare in one small place: Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, three red grapes, vin jaune, sparkling wine and mistelle all coexist without meaning the same thing.

sections.label: Physical place
sections.statement: The Jura vineyard forms a narrow north–south band along the western foothills of the Jura mountains, with varied slopes and exposures rather than one uniform site.

sections.label: How to read the hierarchy
sections.statement: Arbois, Côtes du Jura, L’Etoile and Château-Chalon are geographic AOPs; Crémant du Jura and Macvin du Jura overlap that geography but govern different wine categories and methods.

sections.label: The wine picture
sections.statement: Côtes du Jura permits white, red, rosé and vin jaune; Crémant du Jura is traditional-method sparkling wine; Macvin du Jura is a white, red or rosé liqueur wine. These are distinct legal styles, not interchangeable labels.

quantities.label: A corridor, not a hill

quantity.scope: Communes in the Saint-Joseph geographic area recorded by the specification

quantities.statement: The geographic area covers 26 communes — 23 in the Ardèche and three in the Loire — strung over roughly sixty kilometres of right bank. One appellation name therefore covers a long sequence of different slopes rather than a single côte.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Saint-Joseph was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 15 June 1956, the last of the eight crus to be created; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: Two colours, three grapes
sections.statement: Saint-Joseph may be red or white. For reds the specification requires Syrah to be at least 90% of the holding's encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne permitted only as accessory varieties in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 10% of the vines, and wines made from both colours must be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés". Whites come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: An outline that moved twice
sections.statement: The specification records Saint-Joseph beginning in 1956 on six communes around Tournon, expanding in 1969 by twenty further communes reaching north to the Condrieu area, and then being significantly narrowed by parcel revisions approved on 9–10 February 1994 and 20 June 2018, which cut the delimited parcel area from about 6,800 to about 3,400 hectares. Today's outline is a made thing, not a timeless one.

quantities.statement: The geographic area covers 26 communes — 23 in the Ardèche and three in the Loire — strung over roughly sixty kilometres of right bank. One appellation name therefore covers a long sequence of different slopes rather than a single côte.

quantities.label: Cru appellations

quantity.scope: Cru appellations of the Rhône corridor between Vienne and Valence governed by CARTA

quantities.statement: CARTA governs eight cru appellations in the corridor.

sections.label: What the region is
sections.statement: Northern Rhône is a collective name for the eight cru appellations of the Rhône corridor between Vienne and Valence — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Cornas and Saint-Péray. Each of those eight is separately delimited by its own specification; no appellation, mention or delimited area named Northern Rhône exists, so CARTA holds the region as an editorial grouping with no legal boundary of its own.

sections.label: One grape, a few hectares
sections.statement: Château-Grillet is a still white wine made from Viognier alone, over roughly 3.5 hectares in the communes of Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône and Vérin in the Loire department.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: Condrieu is a still white wine and its specification states plainly that "les vins sont issus du cépage viognier B" — Viognier and nothing else.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

sections.label: What it may be
sections.statement: Côte-Rôtie may only be a still red wine.

sections.label: Two colours, three grapes
sections.statement: Crozes-Hermitage may be red or white. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne admitted as accessory varieties in mixed plantings up to 15% of the vines; whites are Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: Red, white and a third form
sections.statement: Hermitage may be red or white, and white wines may additionally carry the vin de paille mention. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement with Marsanne and Roussanne as accessory varieties; whites and vin de paille come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: Which bank
sections.statement: Six of the eight crus sit on the Rhône's right, western bank — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Cornas and Saint-Péray — while Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage sit on the left bank around Tain-l'Hermitage. Bank is an orientation fact and nothing more: it does not predict landform, substrate or permitted grape.

sections.label: Two colours, three grapes
sections.statement: Saint-Joseph may be red or white. For reds the specification requires Syrah to be at least 90% of the holding's encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne permitted only as accessory varieties in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 10% of the vines, and wines made from both colours must be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés". Whites come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

sections.label: Still and sparkling
sections.statement: Saint-Péray is a white-wine appellation covering both "vins blancs tranquilles" and "vins blancs mousseux", the sparkling wines made by a second fermentation in bottle, from Marsanne and Roussanne, over the communes of Saint-Péray and Toulaud in the Ardèche. INAO gives sparkling wine as roughly a tenth of the volume.

sections.label: Sweetness is a range
sections.statement: The specification's own account describes a wine that was doux in the mid-nineteenth century and is in most cases sec, sometimes demi-sec, in its modern form, with confidential quantities of moelleux or doux made from overripe grapes when conditions allow. "Dry white Viognier" is therefore the usual case, not the legal definition.

sections.label: Permitted grapes
sections.statement: Syrah is the principal variety and must be at least 80% of the holding's encépagement; Viognier is the accessory variety, permitted in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 20% of the vines. Where both varieties are used the specification requires that the wine be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés" — assembled at the grape stage in the same proportion, not blended as finished wines.

sections.label: What vin de paille requires
sections.statement: The vin de paille mention requires the grapes to be dried for at least 45 days between harvest and pressing, a minimum natural richness of 170 grams of sugar per litre — about 19.5% potential alcohol — and a yield of 15 hectolitres per hectare.

sections.label: The ground
sections.statement: The specification describes sandy soils derived from primary-era granite, locally enriched with fine material beneath the château, over a fractured subsoil.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area runs across seven communes and three departments: Condrieu in the Rhône; Chavanay, Malleval, Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf and Vérin in the Loire; and Limony in the Ardèche. INAO gives the vineyard as roughly 100 hectares of terraced right-bank hillside.

sections.label: The amphitheatre
sections.statement: The specification describes most of the vineyard as sitting on soils weathered from primary eruptive rock of the granite family — the porphyritic granites of Tournon — in an amphitheatre open to the south and sheltered from the north by the Arlettes massif, terraced behind stone walls.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area covers Ampuis, Saint-Cyr-sur-le-Rhône and Tupin-et-Semons in the Rhône department, on the right bank south of Vienne, where INAO records slopes steepening to 60% and terraces held by stone walls locally called cheys.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area covers eleven Drôme communes on the left bank facing Tournon — Beaumont-Monteux, Chanos-Curson, Crozes-Hermitage, Erôme, Gervans, Larnage, Pont-de-l'Isère, La Roche-de-Glun, Serves-sur-Rhône, Tain-l'Hermitage and part of Mercurol-Veaunes. It is the largest of the eight crus and the least uniform.

sections.label: Three communes, two appellations
sections.statement: The appellation covers three Drôme communes — Tain-l'Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage and Larnage — on the left bank. The commune named Crozes-Hermitage therefore contains land in both appellations, which is exactly why a commune name cannot tell a reader which wine a parcel may make.

sections.label: Eight rulebooks, twenty years
sections.statement: The eight crus were recognised across two decades and never as one act: Château-Grillet and Saint-Péray by decrees of 8 December 1936, Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage on 4 March 1937 (Hermitage having first been recognised as an appellation d'origine by a judgment of the tribunal de Valence on 25 June 1936), Cornas on 5 August 1938, Condrieu on 27 April 1940, Côte-Rôtie on 18 October 1940 and Saint-Joseph only on 15 June 1956. Different dates froze different rules.

sections.label: The ground
sections.statement: The specification describes a primary granitic basement of the Massif Central, secondary limestone deposits that left the Crussol massif standing, and soils that combine calcareous, clay-limestone and granitic material where the Rhône later carved a collapse basin.

sections.label: Two different grounds
sections.statement: The specification splits the appellation in two. In the north the Rhône has cut down to the granite de Tournon between Crozes-Hermitage and Serves-sur-Rhône, and sandy clays and granitic arenas are held on the slopes by dry-stone terraces. In the south and east lie Quaternary terraces of alpine gravels, with loess locally at the Gervans quartier of Les Blancs and distinctive kaolin sands at Larnage.

sections.label: The broader legal background
sections.statement: The regional Côtes du Rhône AOP extends along the valley from the Vienne sector towards Avignon and overlaps the northern corridor. It is the legal home of fruit that the crus do not cover, which is why a vineyard can sit among the crus and still be sold under a broader name.

sections.label: Appellation, estate, owner
sections.statement: Artémis Domaines records that the Pinault family acquired Château Grillet in 2011 and describes it as one of the very few French monopole AOCs and one of the smallest. The specification's own historical account describes continuous ownership by a single family line from 1830, which is a statement about the estate's past, not about its ownership today.

sections.label: Near-disappearance and recovery
sections.statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.

sections.label: One commune becomes eleven
sections.statement: The 1937 decree limited the area to part of the single commune of Crozes-Hermitage; postwar prosperity and vineyard expansion took it to eleven communes by 1952. A later reselection of the parcels from which grapes may come cut the production potential from 4,800 to 3,200 hectares.

sections.label: Four grapes, eight settings
sections.statement: Four grapes carry the whole corridor: Syrah is the only red variety permitted in any of the five red crus, Viognier is the sole variety of Condrieu and Château-Grillet and the only white admitted into a Côte-Rôtie red, and Marsanne and Roussanne are the white pair of Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray. The same four varieties are re-weighted by each specification rather than by geography.

sections.label: An outline that moved twice
sections.statement: The specification records Saint-Joseph beginning in 1956 on six communes around Tournon, expanding in 1969 by twenty further communes reaching north to the Condrieu area, and then being significantly narrowed by parcel revisions approved on 9–10 February 1994 and 20 June 2018, which cut the delimited parcel area from about 6,800 to about 3,400 hectares. Today's outline is a made thing, not a timeless one.

sections.label: Where the bubbles came from
sections.statement: The Saint-Péray specification traces bottle-fermentation experiments to a merchant's cellarmaster in 1730 and records Louis-Alexandre Faure conducting systematic trials on a hundred barrels in 1828, an innovation it describes as unique in the Rhône valley at the time.

sections.label: A rule change in progress
sections.statement: A modification of the Saint-Péray specification was adopted by the Comité national des appellations d'origine relatives aux vins et aux boissons alcoolisées on 6 February 2025 and placed in the national opposition procedure. A proposal in opposition is not law: CARTA records it as a dated observation and does not present it as the rule in force.

sections.label: Where geology and law disagree
sections.statement: The Crozes-Hermitage specification identifies its northern granite as the same formation that appears across the Rhône around Tournon, in Saint-Joseph. Geology crosses the river and the appellation boundary; the law does not.

sections.label: How to read the map
sections.statement: The active outlines in this world are INAO cartographic representations of eight regulatory geographical areas. They are not vineyard land, not parcel eligibility and not a Northern Rhône polygon; the region label is a derived orientation anchor over the mapped crus.

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Côte-Rôtie was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 18 October 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024, published in the Journal officiel on 7 July 2024.

sections.label: What it may be
sections.statement: Côte-Rôtie may only be a still red wine.

sections.label: Permitted grapes
sections.statement: Syrah is the principal variety and must be at least 80% of the holding's encépagement; Viognier is the accessory variety, permitted in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 20% of the vines. Where both varieties are used the specification requires that the wine be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés" — assembled at the grape stage in the same proportion, not blended as finished wines.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area covers Ampuis, Saint-Cyr-sur-le-Rhône and Tupin-et-Semons in the Rhône department, on the right bank south of Vienne, where INAO records slopes steepening to 60% and terraces held by stone walls locally called cheys.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Château-Grillet was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936, making it one of the corridor's two oldest cru recognitions; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: One grape, a few hectares
sections.statement: Château-Grillet is a still white wine made from Viognier alone, over roughly 3.5 hectares in the communes of Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône and Vérin in the Loire department.

sections.label: The ground
sections.statement: The specification describes sandy soils derived from primary-era granite, locally enriched with fine material beneath the château, over a fractured subsoil.

sections.label: Appellation, estate, owner
sections.statement: Artémis Domaines records that the Pinault family acquired Château Grillet in 2011 and describes it as one of the very few French monopole AOCs and one of the smallest. The specification's own historical account describes continuous ownership by a single family line from 1830, which is a statement about the estate's past, not about its ownership today.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Cornas was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 5 August 1938; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

sections.label: The amphitheatre
sections.statement: The specification describes most of the vineyard as sitting on soils weathered from primary eruptive rock of the granite family — the porphyritic granites of Tournon — in an amphitheatre open to the south and sheltered from the north by the Arlettes massif, terraced behind stone walls.

sections.label: Legal recognition
sections.statement: Condrieu was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 27 April 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

sections.label: One colour, one grape
sections.statement: Condrieu is a still white wine and its specification states plainly that "les vins sont issus du cépage viognier B" — Viognier and nothing else.

sections.label: Sweetness is a range
sections.statement: The specification's own account describes a wine that was doux in the mid-nineteenth century and is in most cases sec, sometimes demi-sec, in its modern form, with confidential quantities of moelleux or doux made from overripe grapes when conditions allow. "Dry white Viognier" is therefore the usual case, not the legal definition.

sections.label: Where it is
sections.statement: The geographic area runs across seven communes and three departments: Condrieu in the Rhône; Chavanay, Malleval, Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf and Vérin in the Loire; and Limony in the Ardèche. INAO gives the vineyard as roughly 100 hectares of terraced right-bank hillside.

sections.label: Near-disappearance and recovery
sections.statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.
